creator: Stanislaw Antol, Aishwarya Agrawal, Jiasen Lu, Margaret Mitchell, Dhruv Batra, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Devi Parikh
description: The VQA Dataset consists of both real images from COCO and abstract cartoon images (SYNTH-VQA). The real-image portion (COCO-VQA) contains 614,163 QA pairs with three questions per image and ten answers per question, available in both open-ended and multiple-choice formats. It is one of the largest and most widely used VQA benchmarks.
name: The VQA Dataset
rai:annotationsPerItem: 10 answers per question (from 10 independent annotators); 3 questions per image
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is 83.3% using the AccuracyVQA metric. Inter-human agreement is especially poor for 'Why' questions, with over 59% of these questions having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer. More than 13% of yes/no answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: AMT workers were asked to 'Stump a smart robot' when generating questions for each image. A separate pool of workers generated answers. Each question was answered by 10 independent annotators. The multiple-choice format includes the correct answer, three plausible answers (collected without seeing the image), the top ten most popular answers in the dataset, and randomly selected correct answers for other questions.
rai:dataBiases: COCO-VQA has strong language biases: many questions can be answered without using the image. Image-blind algorithms achieved 49.6% accuracy using the question alone. 'Yes/no' answers span about 38% of all questions, and almost 59% of them are answered with 'yes.' The dataset contains subjective, opinion-seeking questions without single objective answers. More than 13% of yes/no answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators. SYNTH-VQA was designed to reduce natural image biases (e.g., street scenes more likely to have dogs than zebras) by using synthetic images.
rai:dataCollection: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot.' A separate pool of workers were hired to generate answers to the questions. Each question received ten independent answers. The dataset uses real COCO images and synthetic cartoon images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real images from the Microsoft COCO dataset and synthetic cartoon images (SYNTH-VQA). COCO consists of 328,000 images with 91 common object categories.
rai:dataLimitations: COCO-VQA contains many questions answerable without the image due to language biases. It contains subjective/opinion-seeking questions without single correct answers. Yes/no questions are biased toward 'yes' (59%). The evaluation metric (AccuracyVQA) can be gamed and inflates scores. Inter-human agreement is only 83.3%, making 100% accuracy impossible. The dataset does not provide a detailed breakdown of question types, making it difficult to evaluate performance on specific question types.
rai:dataSocialImpact: VQA datasets enable development of systems that can aid blind and visually impaired individuals by answering questions about images. They also advance human-computer interaction and image retrieval. The paper notes that language biases in the dataset could limit deployment of VQA systems in real-world applications.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and evaluating VQA algorithms; benchmarking visual question answering systems; aiding blind and visually impaired individuals; improving human-computer interaction; image retrieval; Visual Turing Test for image understanding.

evidence.name: The VQA Dataset [32] consists of both real images from COCO and abstract cartoon images. Most work on this dataset has focused solely on the portion containing real world imagery from COCO, which we refer to as COCO-VQA.
evidence.description: COCO-VQA consists of three questions per image, with ten answers per question. Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions. Compared to other VQA datasets, COCO-VQA consists of a relatively large number of questions (614,163 total, with 248,349 for training, 121,512 for validation, and 244,302 for testing).

evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The VQA Dataset [32] consists of both real images from COCO and abstract cartoon images. With exception of DAQUAR, all of the datasets include images from the Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset [10], which consists of 328,000 images, 91 common object categories with over 2 million labeled instances, and an average of 5 captions per image.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: COCO-VQA has a large variety of questions, but many of them can be accurately answered without using the image due to language biases. Relatively simple image-blind algorithms have achieved 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA using the question alone. The dataset also contains many subjective, opinion-seeking questions that do not have a single objective answer. 'yes/no' answers span about 38% of all questions, and almost 59% of them are answered with 'yes.'
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Using AccuracyVQA, the inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is only 83.3%. It is impossible for an algorithm to achieve 100% accuracy. Inter-human agreement is especially poor for 'Why' questions, with over 59% of these questions having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: COCO-VQA has a large variety of questions, but many of them can be accurately answered without using the image due to language biases. Relatively simple image-blind algorithms have achieved 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA using the question alone. The dataset also contains many subjective, opinion-seeking questions that do not have a single objective answer.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. More generally, VQA could be used to improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content. A VQA system can also be used for image retrieval, without using image meta-data or tags.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. For example, as a blind user scrolls through their social media feed, a captioning system can describe the image and then the user could use VQA to query the image to get more insight about the scene.
evidence.isLiveDataset: Beginning in 2014, five major datasets for VQA have been publicly released. These datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated. As of this article, the main datasets for VQA are DAQUAR, COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset, FM-IQA, Visual7W, and Visual Genome.
